question.leadin: Answer the following about the Gaza Strip.
question.text: In 1993, Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed a series of accords named for this city, the capital of Norway. The accords gave Palestinians the right to self-government in Gaza.
question.clue: Works such as Monolith, which is a tower of human bodies, and Wheel of Life are contained in this city's Frogner Park, which features other stone and bronze statuary by Gustav Vigeland .

swap.leadin: Answer the following about German invasions during World War II.
swap.text: Germany invaded this country and Denmark as part of Operation Weserubung. This country was home to German heavy water production and was led by Vidkun Quisling after its surrender.
swap.clue: In 1905, it elected Prince Carl as its king, breaking up a union that had been forced since the Treaty of Kiel.

question.leadin: The Treaty of Nystad ended this war in 1721, 12 years after a decisive victory over Charles XII at Poltava ended Sweden's time as a European power.
question.text: Name this war motivated by one European power's desire for a port city on the Baltic Sea.
question.clue: During this war, one side relieved a siege during a snowstorm at the Battle of Narva.

swap.leadin: This member of the House of Vasa defeated Count Tilly in his most famous victory, Breitenfeld.
swap.text: Name this man who died at the Battle of Lutzen and was known as the "Lion of the North."
swap.answerHtml: Gustavus Adolphus [or Gustav Adolf; Gustav II; Gustavus the Great; prompt on “Gustav” or “Gustavus”]
swap.clue: In addition to ending the Kalmar War, one military rival to this person employed an elector named Maximilian I that died with him at Ingolstadt after losing to the numerically superior force of this ruler at the Battle of the Rain.

question.leadin: The author of the Prose Edda, Snorri Sturluson, was a law speaker of a parliament in this country.
question.text: Name this country home to the Althing, the oldest European parliament that is still functioning.
question.clue: In 1986, Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan met at a summit in this country's capital city that eventually resulted in the signing of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty.

swap.leadin: This man was exiled after his slaves started a landslide on his neighbor's farm.
swap.text: Name this man who established the first Norse community in Greenland, misleadingly naming it to attract settlers.
swap.clue: During that exile, he established an estate at Brattahlith.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of paper money.
question.text: This European country was the first to print paper money, doing so from its central bank during the reign of Carl Gustaf. That central bank was based out of this country's capital at Stockholm.
question.clue: A ruler of this kingdom launched a successful coup in 1772 against his own parliament, effectively ending the power of the Francophilic Hats and the Russophilic Caps.

swap.leadin: This institution was formed when Margaret I of Denmark's great-nephew, Erik of Pomerania, was crowned on Trinity Sunday.
swap.text: Name this Nordic union established to counter the influence of the Hanseatic League. Internal conflict in this polity occurred primarily between Danish and Swedish "protectors of the realm" such as Sten Sture the Elder.
swap.clue: Members of the Sture family served as regents to this state, which was targeted by the Engelbrekt rising.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about Nazi collaborationist governments.
question.text: The Nazis also replaced Johann Nygaardsvold with this leader of the Nasjonal Samling party, who governed with Josef Terboven.
question.clue: This politician launched their political career in a series of articles explaining their 'political thoughts' on the death of mentor Fritjohf Nansen.

swap.text: In the 1920s, the League of Nations notably arbitrated Finland's dispute with Sweden over these islands in the mouth of the Gulf of Bothnia. The League found them to be over 90% Swedish in population, and thus naturally awarded them to Finland.
swap.clue: This archipelago in the Baltic Sea that was the subject of a dispute between Sweden and Finland that ended with these islands of Swedes staying Finnish but becoming mostly autonomous.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about the history of some islands in Europe that are not Great Britain or Ireland.
question.text: This Norwegian territory's namesake treaty regulates commercial and military activities. This Arctic archipelago is home to one of the largest seed banks in the world -- the Global Seed Vault.
question.answerHtml: Svalbard [prompt on Spitsbergen; do NOT accept or prompt on “Jan Mayen”]
question.clue: The name of this Norwegian archipelago means "cold shores," and its three inhabited islands are Spitzbergen, Bear Island, and Hopen.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about weird deaths.
swap.text: This Danish scientist and author of Introduction to the New Astronomy died after contracting a kidney ailment that was brought on by a banquet in which he refused to leave the table to relieve himself so as to avoid committing a social faux pas.
swap.clue: This scientist who constructed the Uraniborg observatory as Lord of Hven. He wore a brass nose after losing a duel.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of the good old-fashioned fun of throwing sticks.
question.text: The stick throwing game of skittles originated in a region this country shares with its eastern neighbour. A bat sport invented by a veteran of this country's Civil War was demonstrated when it hosted the 1952 Summer Olympics.
question.clue: Principles surrounding the ethics of human experimentation were codified in a declaration signed in this country, which lends its name to a process in which a small country adopts a larger neighbor's foreign policy prerogatives.

swap.leadin: Construction on this fortification began after the signing of the Treaty of Tartu in 1920, which established a border between two countries on the Karelian Isthmus.
swap.text: Name this defensive fortification constructed between Taipale and the Gulf of Finland.
swap.clue: Reinforced concrete and protection plates were dropped from this due to a rise in the price of steel, and parts of it were simply strategically placed mounds of soil known as "slope cuts."

question.leadin: The Angers Fragment is the only surviving portion of a text by this historian that is confirmed to be written in his handwriting.
question.text: Name this historian who received the patronage of Absalon. In the 12th century, this historian wrote about the legendary warrior Starkad and the king Amleth.
question.clue: This historian discusses rulers up to the time of Canute VI in his Gesta Danorum, which he likely composed under Danish king Valdemar I.

swap.leadin: This ship was salvaged in 1961, over 300 years after sinking on its maiden voyage.
swap.text: Name this ship, now housed at a namesake museum in Stockholm. This ship shares its name with the dynasty of its commissioner, who was advised by Axel Oxenstierna.
swap.clue: A queen from this royal house abdicated after converting to Catholicism and housed Descartes in his final years.

question.leadin: Answer the following about insane CIA Cold War plots that did not involve exploding cigars or acoustic kitties.
question.text: This place was long thought to contain a lost hydrogen bomb after a secret mission crashed at Thule Air Base. Project Iceworm wanted to build launch sites under this territory of Denmark, which is the world's largest island.
question.clue: Henrik Kauffman signed a 1941 treaty with the United States paving the way for the establishment of Thule Airbase on this island.

swap.leadin: There is debate as to whether these warriors fought bare-chested or wore wolf skins.
swap.text: Identify these bear-worshiping Norse fighters named for their bouts of induced craziness.
swap.clue: You were probably really scared of these Viking warriors who supposedly fought in a trance like state and wore horned helmets as the specially chosen warriors of Odin.

question.text: Name this founder of the Vasa dynasty who signed the Treaty of Malmo with Christian II, thus relieving Sweden of Denmark's rule in the Kalmar Union.
